rationale: Evidence: iteration 7 (sensors moved forward to y = 0.06 m) is the best design so far at 654.8, up from 384.9 at y = 0.03 m. The oval finishes 20 of 20 at 1.91 s with rms 0.005 m. The s-bend finishes 18 of 20 (mean 868). The slalom still fails in all 20 trials by going off track, with progress 0.35 and about 1.1 line-loss events per run. Steering oscillation is moderate (0.22 oval, 0.43 s-bend, 0.24 slalom). Forward sensor position is the only lever that has produced a large gain: it moved the sensors from 0.03 to 0.06 m ahead of the axle and added about 307 points. Earlier levers (base_speed, sensor spacing, sensor size, kp/kd at 3.5/1.0) either had no effect or hurt. Change (one variable): move all five sensors from y = 0.06 m to y = 0.08 m, the upper geometry limit. Geometry x positions, sensor size, wheel_track, mass and all controller values stay as in iteration 7. The added look-ahead should reduce the lag at direction changes that causes slalom line losses. Expected result: slalom progress rises (goal above 0.5) with fewer line-loss events, the oval still finishes at about 1.9 to 2.0 s, and s-bend completions hold or improve. Risk: the loop may become less stable, which would show as steering_oscillation above about 0.5 on the s-bend. If that happens, the next step is to lower kp slightly (to about 2.7) at y = 0.08 rather than reverting the sensor move. Hypotheses to check: (a) the slalom failure is lag at the first sign change, so more look-ahead recovers progress; (b) if progress does not move beyond the y = 0.06 result, the limit is the steering response and the next test should change wheel_track or mass alone. Next measurements: progress, line_loss_events, max_error and steering_oscillation per track, plus completion_time on the oval and s-bend.
